title: Warnings That Went Unheeded
overview: Amos condemns the wealthy of Samaria for crushing the poor and for showy worship, lists disasters Israel lived through without changing, and warns that they must now face God himself.

parts.label: The cows of Bashan (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Bashan was known for fat, well fed cattle, and Amos, once a herdsman, uses the image for the rich women of Samaria, the northern capital, whose luxury was paid for by crushing the poor. He warns they will be hauled out through broken city walls like fish on hooks, possibly echoing how Assyrians led captives by hooks, though where Harmon was is unknown.

parts.label: Worship as showing off (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Bethel and Gilgal were major shrines in the northern kingdom, and Amos mockingly tells people to go there and do wrong, because their busy rituals came with no justice. The law did not allow bread made with yeast to be burned on the altar, and bragging about voluntary gifts turned worship into a display.

parts.label: Hunger, drought and crop loss (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: God is described as sending famine, rain on one town but not the next, blight, mildew and locusts, each meant as a signal to turn back. Every round ends with the same sad line: they still did not come back to God.

parts.label: Plague, war and near destruction (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: The list grows harsher: disease like the plagues of Egypt, young men killed in battle, the stench of the dead in camp, and places overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah. The text says plainly that God brought these things, and that Israel survived only like a burning stick pulled from a fire.

parts.label: A meeting with God (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: Since nothing else changed them, Israel must now get ready to face God directly, and the threat is left unnamed, which makes it more ominous. The closing lines, likely from a hymn, describe the one who shapes mountains, makes the wind and turns dawn to darkness, and who makes thoughts known to people, a line that can mean either God's own thoughts or theirs.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the call to get ready to meet God is a final sentence of doom or a last urgent invitation to turn back while there is still time.
think: When hard times come, what tends to make a person or a society change course, and what tends to make them dig in?
